lessonTitle: CT Anatomy: Axial Thorax, Abdomen and Head

blocks.text: A 68-year-old man on an anticoagulant is found drowsy after a fall. Within minutes of arriving, he is in the scanner. On the screen, a bright crescent hugs the inside of his skull on one side. That white crescent is blood, and the reason it looks white lies in how CT turns X-ray attenuation into grey levels.

blocks.markdown: In computed tomography (CT) an X-ray tube rotates around the patient and detectors measure how much the beam is attenuated along many paths. A computer reconstructs thin **axial** slices. By convention you view each slice **from the patient's feet**, so the patient's right is on the left of the image and anterior is at the top.

blocks.title: Hounsfield unit (HU)
blocks.text: A scale of CT attenuation that sets distilled water at 0 HU and air at -1000 HU. A tissue with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu$ has a CT number given by the formula below, where $\mu_{\text{water}}$ is the coefficient of water.

blocks.caption: Hounsfield scale. Denser tissue attenuates more and appears whiter.

blocks.title: From attenuation coefficient to Hounsfield units
blocks.prompt: A tissue has $\mu = 0.205\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and water has $\mu_{\text{water}} = 0.190\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ at the same beam energy. Find its HU.

steps.text: Write the formula and substitute the values.
Subtract water attenuation from tissue attenuation, then divide by water.
A value of about 79 HU is denser than water and in the range of clotted blood or enhanced soft tissue.

blocks.caption: Typical values; they vary slightly with scanner, patient and kVp.

blocks.markdown: **Contrast.** Intravenous iodinated contrast raises the attenuation of anything it perfuses, so **vessels become bright** (arteries immediately, veins later) and highly vascular organs enhance. Timing the scan gives phases: the arterial phase shows bright aorta and arteries, while the portal venous phase shows enhancing liver, spleen and kidneys with opacified veins. The same contrast can be given orally to outline the gut. Contrast is avoided or used with care in significant renal impairment or a history of serious contrast allergy.

blocks.title: Measuring enhancement
blocks.prompt: A region in the liver measures 55 HU before contrast and 110 HU in the portal venous phase. By how much did it enhance, and why can a vessel and a thrombus be told apart?

steps.text: Enhancement is the post-contrast value minus the pre-contrast value.
Contrast fills a patent lumen and makes it bright, whereas a thrombus does not receive contrast and remains at its lower pre-contrast attenuation, producing a filling defect.

blocks.answer: Enhancement is 55 HU; thrombus appears as a filling defect.

blocks.markdown: **Axial anatomy.** In the thorax, scroll from top to bottom to meet the aortic arch, then the ascending and descending aorta with the pulmonary trunk, then the left atrium and the four heart chambers. The lungs are black with branching vessels, and the oesophagus lies behind the left atrium. In the upper abdomen the liver lies on the left of the image (the patient's right) and the stomach and spleen on the right of the image, the aorta lies just left of the midline in front of the vertebral body, and the inferior vena cava lies to the right of the midline. At lower levels the kidneys sit on either side of the spine, and the pancreas lies in front of the aorta and splenic vein.

items: Orient the image: patient's right is on the left of the screen.
Name the level using the vertebra, aorta and lungs.
Identify the major vessels first, with the aorta left and IVC right of midline.
Then identify solid organs: liver, spleen, kidneys, pancreas.
Finish with bowel, bones and soft tissues.

blocks.markdown: **Intracranial haemorrhage on non-contrast CT.** Fresh clotted blood has a high attenuation and is **hyperdense** (bright) against brain. An **extradural** haematoma is biconvex or lens-shaped and does not cross suture lines. A **subdural** haematoma is crescentic and spreads across the surface of the hemisphere, crossing sutures but not the falx. **Subarachnoid** blood outlines the basal cisterns and sulci. Over days, haemorrhage loses attenuation and becomes isodense and later hypodense.

rows: Limited by sutures; can cross the falx
Crosses sutures; limited by the falx
Follows the brain surface and basal cisterns
blocks.caption: Acute extra-axial haemorrhage on non-contrast CT.

blocks.title: Non-contrast first for the head
blocks.text: A non-contrast head CT is used to detect acute haemorrhage because blood is bright and contrast would confuse the picture of blood versus enhancement.

blocks.title: Window settings matter
blocks.text: Brain, lung and bone are viewed with different windows (level and width). A small subdural may be missed at a brain window set too narrow or wide, so scroll through the images at suitable settings.

points: HU = 1000 times (mu minus mu water) over mu water; water is 0 HU and air is -1000 HU.
Contrast brightens vessels and enhancing organs; a thrombus appears as a filling defect.
Acute blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT: extradural lens-shaped, subdural crescentic, subarachnoid in cisterns and sulci.

questions.stem: A tissue has linear attenuation coefficient 0.1862 per cm and water has 0.1900 per cm. Calculate the CT number in Hounsfield units using $\text{HU} = 1000(\mu - \mu_w)/\mu_w$.
questions.explanation: (0.1862 - 0.1900)/0.1900 = -0.02, and multiplying by 1000 gives -20 HU. A value slightly below zero is consistent with fat-containing or low-density material and is lower than water.

questions.stem: On a standard axial CT slice displayed in the usual convention, where is the patient's right side?

options.text: On the left of the image
On the right of the image
At the top of the image
At the bottom of the image

questions.correctOptionText: On the left of the image

distractorRationale.a: Correct: axial slices are viewed from the feet so the right side appears on the left.
distractorRationale.b: This would be the left-right reversal.
distractorRationale.c: Top of the image is anterior.
distractorRationale.d: Bottom of the image is posterior.

questions.explanation: Axial images are viewed as if looking up from the patient's feet, so the patient's right is on the left of the screen. Anterior is at the top.

questions.stem: At the level of the upper abdomen on an axial CT, which vessel lies just left of the midline in front of the vertebral body?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the aorta lies just left of the midline in front of the vertebra.
distractorRationale.b: The IVC lies to the right of the midline.
distractorRationale.c: The superior mesenteric vein lies in front of the aorta and the pancreas head region, not directly on the vertebra.
distractorRationale.d: The left renal vein passes in front of the aorta, not alongside the vertebral body.

questions.explanation: The aorta descends slightly left of the midline, anterior to the vertebral bodies, while the IVC lies to its right. Remembering this pair quickly orients you on any abdominal slice.

questions.stem: A pre-contrast CT shows a vessel lumen at 40 HU and the post-contrast arterial phase shows the same lumen at 320 HU. What explains the change?

options.text: Iodinated contrast within the blood increased attenuation

questions.correctOptionText: Iodinated contrast within the blood increased attenuation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: iodine strongly attenuates X-rays and brightens the lumen.
distractorRationale.b: Wall thickening would not change the lumen density.
distractorRationale.c: Motion causes blurring, not uniform brightening.
distractorRationale.d: Air would reduce attenuation, making it darker.

questions.explanation: Iodine contrast attenuates X-rays strongly, so perfused vessels become bright. The measured rise in HU reflects contrast within the blood.

questions.stem: A renal lesion measures 30 HU before contrast and 85 HU after intravenous contrast. By how many Hounsfield units has it enhanced?
questions.explanation: Enhancement equals the post-contrast value minus the pre-contrast value, 85 minus 30 = 55 HU. A rise of this order shows that the lesion is perfused with contrast.

questions.stem: A contrast-enhanced scan shows a pulmonary artery branch with a dark central area surrounded by a bright rim. What does this most likely represent?

options.text: A filling defect from thrombus within the vessel

questions.correctOptionText: A filling defect from thrombus within the vessel

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unenhanced thrombus appears dark inside a bright lumen.
distractorRationale.b: Air is not expected in the artery.
distractorRationale.c: Calcified plaque would be brighter than contrast, not darker.

questions.explanation: Contrast fills the patent lumen and renders it bright, so a thrombus that does not enhance forms a filling defect. This is how emboli or clots in vessels are recognised.

questions.stem: A non-contrast head CT in a 45-year-old shows a lens-shaped hyperdense collection against the inner table of the temporal bone, which does not cross the coronal suture. This is most consistent with:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: biconvex hyperdensity limited by the sutures is extradural.
distractorRationale.b: Subdural is crescentic and crosses sutures.
distractorRationale.c: Subarachnoid blood fills the sulci and cisterns.
distractorRationale.d: A chronic infarct appears hypodense, not hyperdense.

questions.explanation: An extradural collection is biconvex because the dura is adherent at the sutures. Fresh blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT.

questions.stem: On non-contrast CT, which appearance best matches an acute subdural haematoma?

options.text: Crescent of hyperdensity spreading over the hemisphere
Hyperdense cast of the basal cisterns

questions.correctOptionText: Crescent of hyperdensity spreading over the hemisphere

distractorRationale.a: Correct: crescentic hyperdensity crossing sutures is subdural.

questions.explanation: A subdural collection lies between the dura and arachnoid and spreads across the hemisphere in a crescent. It can cross suture lines but not the falx.

questions.stem: Explain why a non-contrast scan is used first to look for acute intracranial haemorrhage and why contrast is useful for vascular assessment.
markingGuide: Acute blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT.
Contrast would brighten vessels and enhancing tissue, possibly masking or mimicking blood.
Contrast raises attenuation of perfused structures so vessels are shown.
Avoid contrast in renal impairment or allergy.
questions.explanation: Blood is already bright, so contrast adds nothing for haemorrhage and can confuse the picture. For vessels, contrast opacifies the lumen and highlights obstruction.

questions.stem: Describe how you would orient yourself on an axial CT slice of the upper abdomen and name the main structures you would identify.
markingGuide: Patient's right on the left of the image, anterior at top.
Aorta left of midline in front of the vertebra; IVC to the right.
Spleen and stomach on the image-right.
Kidneys and pancreas at appropriate levels.
questions.explanation: A fixed orientation lets you place organs correctly. The aorta and vertebra are used as anchors, and the liver on the patient's right confirms the orientation.
